ProdFlow

Product Development & Supplier Management Platform. UX/UI case study, Enterprise SaaS

01. Overview02. The Problem03. Initial Findings04. Goals05. The Solution06. Design Process07. Test & Launch08. Outcome09. Reflection

01. Overview

THE PROJECT

Bringing a physical product from concept to market involves multiple teams, suppliers, revisions, and approvals. Yet much of this information is often spread across spreadsheets, emails, and disconnected tools.

ProdFlow explores how a centralized digital workspace can make product development more organized, transparent, and efficient.

Designed for product designers, development managers, and sourcing teams, the platform brings together product tracking, supplier comparisons, sample reviews, cost management, and risk monitoring in one place.

Scattered tools, one workspace

SpreadsheetsEmailsSupplier quotesSample feedbackBOM filesPackaging files
ProdFlow
My roleProduct Designer: UX Research, Information Architecture, UI Design, Prototyping
Project typeEnterprise SaaS / B2B Product Design
DeliverableInteractive web application prototype

02. The Problem

UNDERSTANDING THE CHALLENGE

How might we help product development teams manage complex workflows without losing track of critical information, decisions, and deadlines?

Developing physical products requires constant coordination between design, engineering, sourcing, manufacturing, and compliance teams. When information is scattered across multiple platforms, even small changes can create confusion and delays.

Fragmented information

Product specifications, supplier quotes, and sample feedback are stored across different tools.

Limited visibility

Teams struggle to understand product progress, outstanding approvals, and upcoming deadlines.

Difficult supplier decisions

Comparing cost, quality, lead times, and manufacturing capabilities requires manual effort.

Revision confusion

Multiple versions of samples, BOMs, and packaging files make it difficult to identify the latest approved information.

Reactive problem-solving

Potential manufacturing delays, cost overruns, and compliance issues may be discovered too late.

These challenges informed the need for a connected system that supports both day-to-day execution and better decision-making.

03. Initial Findings

DISCOVERING OPPORTUNITIES

Drawing from physical product development workflows, I identified several recurring challenges that shaped the initial design direction.

01. Information needs a single source of truth.

Teams need one place to access product specifications, revision histories, supplier information, and current project status.

02. Decisions require context, not just data.

Supplier selection involves balancing cost, quality, lead time, and reliability rather than simply choosing the lowest quote.

03. Feedback should be actionable.

Sample reviews need clearly documented issues, severity levels, ownership, and revision tracking to reduce miscommunication.

04. Risks should be visible before they become problems.

Cost changes, delayed samples, and missing compliance approvals need to be surfaced early enough for teams to take action.

These are preliminary workflow insights and design hypotheses, not findings from a documented user research study.

04. Goals

DEFINING SUCCESS

The primary goal was to create an intuitive, connected workspace that reduces the complexity of managing physical product development. The design focused on four objectives.

Improve visibility

Give teams a clear overview of product progress, responsibilities, deadlines, and outstanding tasks.

Simplify workflows

Connect supplier sourcing, BOM management, sample reviews, and approvals within a consistent experience.

Support informed decisions

Present comparable supplier data, cost changes, and evidence-backed risk information.

Increase accountability

Make ownership, feedback, approval status, and production readiness easier to track.

05. The Solution

INTRODUCING PRODFLOW

ProdFlow brings the product development lifecycle into one structured workspace, helping teams move from scattered information to connected workflows. The solution centers around six key experiences.

How it works

A quick look at four moments in the product: finding priorities, choosing a supplier, reviewing a sample, and acting on a risk.

PFProdFlow
  • Home
  • Products
  • Suppliers
  • RFQs
  • Samples
  • Approvals

  • Risks

Side-by-side supplier comparison

Teams can compare supplier quotations across unit cost, minimum order quantity, tooling costs, lead times, and quality performance, while documenting the reasoning behind their decisions.

06. Design Process

FROM COMPLEXITY TO CLARITY

01Discover
02Define
03Structure
04Design
05Prototype

Discover: understanding the workflow

I began by breaking down the physical product development journey, from initial concept and supplier sourcing to sampling, approvals, and production. This helped identify the information, decisions, and dependencies that needed to remain connected throughout the process.

Define: prioritizing user needs

I translated the workflow challenges into core product requirements: clear project visibility, centralized information, traceable revisions, structured feedback, and actionable risk alerts. Rather than designing separate tools for each task, I focused on how these activities could work together.

Structure: building the information architecture

I organized the platform around the primary areas users would need to access: Products, Suppliers, RFQs, Samples, Approvals, and Risks. Each product acts as a central workspace, allowing users to move between related information without losing context.

Design: making complex data easier to understand

I used a clean enterprise interface with consistent tables, status indicators, lifecycle trackers, and contextual actions. Special attention was given to visual hierarchy, helping users distinguish urgent tasks from general information and understand the next step without unnecessary navigation.

Prototype: connecting the experience

I developed an interactive web prototype around a sample product, LoopRace Travel Game, to demonstrate the complete workflow. It includes supplier selection, BOM cost calculations, sample issue logging, approval decisions, and risk status management. This made it possible to explore how decisions in one part of the product development process connect to other activities.

07. Test & Launch

VALIDATING THE EXPERIENCE

The current project is an interactive prototype designed to demonstrate and evaluate key product development workflows. It can be explored through representative scenarios, including comparing supplier quotations, adding BOM components, reviewing samples, requesting changes, and managing production approvals.

These scenarios provide a foundation for future usability testing, with particular attention to:

  • How quickly users can identify priority tasks.
  • Whether supplier tradeoffs are easy to understand.
  • How clearly users can document and track sample issues.
  • Whether approval statuses and production blockers are understandable.
  • How easily users can navigate between connected workflows.

Current status: Prototype developed; formal usability testing and a live product launch are not documented.

The next stage would involve testing with product designers, sourcing professionals, and product development managers before expanding the platform.

08. Outcome

WHAT THE PROJECT DELIVERED

ProdFlow resulted in an interactive enterprise SaaS prototype that demonstrates how multiple product development activities can be brought together into one connected experience.

0Core workflow areas
0Detailed end-to-end product case
0Supplier quotations to compare
0Risk scenarios demonstrated
  • Connected workflows: Product information, supplier decisions, sample reviews, and approvals can be accessed within a consistent system.
  • Greater decision transparency: Supplier comparisons and risk explanations make supporting information visible rather than presenting unexplained recommendations.
  • Actionable feedback: Visual issue annotations and structured revision tracking show how sample feedback can be communicated more clearly.
  • Production visibility: Readiness checks highlight missing requirements before a product can progress to manufacturing.

These are demonstrated design capabilities, not yet measured improvements in operational efficiency or business performance.

09. Reflection

WHAT I LEARNED

Designing ProdFlow challenged me to think beyond individual screens and consider how an entire product development system works together. One of the biggest takeaways was that simplifying a complex workflow does not mean removing information. It means presenting the right information at the right moment.

The project also reinforced the importance of designing around real decisions. Whether selecting a supplier, reviewing a sample, or approving production, users need context, clarity, and confidence in their next action.

My background in physical product development helped me connect manufacturing processes with digital workflows and explore how thoughtful UX design can reduce friction between teams.

If I were to take this project further, I would focus on validating the experience with real users, refining cross-team collaboration, and developing more robust risk monitoring and supplier communication features.

Ultimately, ProdFlow represents my exploration of how human-centered design can transform complex operational processes into more intuitive and connected digital experiences.

Care Handoff

Making caregiving more connected, organized, and less overwhelming. UX/UI case study, mobile application, healthcare and family care coordination

01. Overview02. Problem03. Initial Findings04. Goals05. Solution06. Design Process07. Test & Launch08. Outcome09. Reflection

01. Overview

THE PROJECT

Caring for a loved one is rarely a one-person responsibility. Family members, professional caregivers, and occasional helpers often work together to manage medications, appointments, daily activities, and changing health needs. However, keeping everyone informed can become challenging when responsibilities are shared across multiple people.

Care Handoff is a mobile care coordination platform designed to bring caregivers together in one organized space. The app helps families track daily care activities, assign responsibilities, communicate important updates, and create structured handoff summaries when caregiving responsibilities change.

The goal was to design an experience that makes caregiving feel less fragmented and more manageable, while helping everyone involved feel informed, supported, and connected.

Project typeConceptual product design
My roleProduct Designer: UX/UI Design, Information Architecture, Interaction Design, Prototyping
DeliverableInteractive mobile application prototype

02. Problem

WHEN CARE IS SHARED, IMPORTANT INFORMATION CAN GET LOST

Caregiving involves much more than completing daily tasks. It requires continuous communication, coordination, and awareness of a loved one's changing needs. In a shared caregiving environment, information may be scattered across text messages, phone calls, personal notes, and individual schedules.

Fragmented communication

Care updates are shared through different channels, making it difficult to find important information.

Unclear responsibilities

Family members may not know who is handling a medication refill, appointment, or household task.

Incomplete handoffs

When one caregiver finishes their responsibilities, the next person may not receive a complete picture of what happened.

Missed health patterns

Individual observations may seem insignificant until they occur repeatedly.

Limited visibility

Family members who are not physically present may struggle to stay informed.

These challenges can increase mental workload and create uncertainty for everyone involved.

How might we help families and caregivers coordinate responsibilities, share important information, and maintain continuity of care without adding more complexity to their daily lives?

03. Initial Findings

UNDERSTANDING THE CAREGIVING EXPERIENCE

I explored common coordination challenges that can arise when multiple people are responsible for supporting one individual. Four key opportunity areas shaped the design direction.

1. Care information needs a shared home.

Caregivers need an easy way to understand what has happened, what is happening, and what still needs attention. Opportunity: a centralized care dashboard and chronological activity timeline.

2. Assigning a task is not the same as confirming responsibility.

A task may be requested, but that does not mean someone has agreed to complete it. Opportunity: clear task states, including unassigned, requested, accepted, and completed.

3. Care transitions require more than a quick message.

The next caregiver needs context about completed activities, unusual observations, outstanding tasks, and upcoming appointments. Opportunity: structured, reviewable handoff summaries from recorded care activities.

4. Repeated observations can reveal important changes.

An individual note about dizziness or discomfort might be easy to overlook. Opportunity: surface recurring patterns alongside the original observations so caregivers can review and discuss them with healthcare professionals.

01Unassigned
02Requested
03Accepted
04Completed

These are preliminary design insights and hypotheses, not findings from documented user interviews or usability research.

04. Goals

The primary goal was to create a calm, intuitive mobile experience that supports caregivers without overwhelming them with information.

User goals

  • Understand a loved one's current care status at a glance.
  • Know which tasks require attention and who is responsible.
  • Record medications, meals, and observations quickly.
  • Share clear handoff summaries between caregivers.
  • Keep relevant family members and professional caregivers informed.
  • Control access to sensitive care information.

Product goals

Clarity

Make critical information easy to find and understand.

Accountability

Establish clear ownership and progress for shared responsibilities.

Continuity

Preserve important context when caregiving responsibilities change.

Collaboration

Support communication across different caregiving roles.

Trust

Give families visibility and control over information-sharing preferences.

05. Solution

ONE SHARED SPACE FOR BETTER CARE COORDINATION

Care Handoff brings daily activities, responsibilities, communication, and care transitions into a connected mobile experience. Rather than asking caregivers to manage several disconnected tools, the interface organizes information around the questions they are most likely to have.

How it works

Four moments in the app: assigning a task, logging an observation, handing off care, and reviewing a pattern.

3:47
HomeTimelineTasksTeamMore

Animated walkthrough recreated from the prototype's screens and sample data.

A. Home dashboard: know what matters now

The home screen provides a quick overview of the care recipient's day. It highlights items needing attention, recently completed activities, and upcoming appointments. The goal is to help caregivers understand what needs their attention within seconds.

Design decision: Prioritize actionable information over displaying every available detail.

B. Care timeline: create a shared record

The timeline organizes care activities chronologically, including medications, meals, observations, appointments, and task updates. Entries identify who recorded the activity, helping provide context and accountability. Caregivers can also add updates through a simplified interaction flow.

Design decision: Use a chronological timeline to make care history easier to scan and follow.

C. Task management: make responsibilities clear

The task system allows caregivers to create, assign, accept, decline, and complete responsibilities. Each task includes its due date, assignee, and current status. Instead of assuming a task is being handled once assigned, the interface distinguishes between a request and an accepted responsibility.

Design decision: Make ownership and progress visible to reduce uncertainty and duplicated effort.

D. Caregiver handoff: transfer context, not just tasks

The handoff experience is the central feature of the concept. When a caregiver is ready to pass responsibilities to someone else, the app prepares a structured summary using recorded daily activities. The caregiver can review the summary before sharing it with the care team.

What a handoff can include

  • ✓Completed activities
  • ✓Health observations
  • ✓Outstanding tasks
  • ✓Upcoming appointments
  • ✓An optional personal note

Design decision: Combine automated organization with human review, allowing caregivers to control what is communicated.

E. Care insights: make patterns easier to notice

The Care Insights screen presents a concept for highlighting recurring observations. For example, the prototype surfaces three recorded dizziness observations and allows the caregiver to review their dates, details, and authors. This helps connect individual entries into a more understandable pattern.

Design decision: Pair a concise insight with supporting observations rather than presenting an unexplained alert.

These insights are intended to support awareness and conversations with healthcare professionals, not provide diagnoses.

F. Care team and permissions: share information thoughtfully

The care team includes different roles, such as family caregivers, professional caregivers, and transportation helpers. The interface allows the care organizer to configure access to medication information, observations, and private family notes.

Design decision: Recognize that not everyone involved in caregiving needs access to the same information.

G. Medications, appointments, and messages: connect everyday workflows

Additional screens support medication schedules and dose logging, upcoming and past appointments, and care team messaging. These functions provide the supporting information needed for the dashboard, timeline, and handoff experience.

Design decision: Keep related workflows within one consistent navigation system so users do not have to switch between multiple tools.

06. Design Process

FROM A SHARED SCENARIO TO A CONNECTED PROTOTYPE

Step 1: Define the care coordination challenge

I started by framing the experience around a shared caregiving scenario involving a care organizer, family members, a professional caregiver, and an occasional helper. This helped identify the different responsibilities and information needs within one care team. The core challenge was not simply storing information. It was ensuring that the right person could understand and act on it at the right time.

Step 2: Map the key workflows

I organized the experience around five connected actions.

01Check status
02Record updates
03Coordinate tasks
04Review changes
05Hand off care

This structure helped determine which information should appear on the home screen and which activities required dedicated views.

Step 3: Establish the information architecture

The primary navigation uses five sections: Home, Timeline, Tasks, Team, and More. Frequently accessed functions are placed directly in the bottom navigation, while supporting tools such as medications, appointments, messages, care insights, and handoff creation are accessible through the More menu. This keeps the primary navigation compact while preserving access to deeper functionality.

Step 4: Design the visual experience

The visual direction focuses on calmness, readability, and clarity. I used a soft blue-green palette, rounded cards, generous spacing, and clear typographic hierarchy to create a reassuring interface. Color-coded indicators distinguish urgent items, upcoming activities, completed tasks, and informational updates. The intention was to make the app feel supportive rather than clinical or overwhelming.

Step 5: Prototype connected interactions

I developed an interactive mobile prototype centered on a sample care recipient, Eleanor, and her caregiving team. It demonstrates task assignment and status changes, activity logging, medication tracking, appointment management, handoff generation, messaging, and configurable permissions. It also includes editable sample data and local browser persistence to support exploration of different workflows.

07. Test & Launch

PROTOTYPE VALIDATION

The project currently demonstrates an interactive concept rather than a publicly launched healthcare application. The prototype allows key interactions to be explored:

  1. Identifying an urgent task from the home dashboard.
  2. Assigning that task to another caregiver.
  3. Recording a care activity or medication dose.
  4. Reviewing a recurring health observation.
  5. Generating and reviewing a caregiver handoff summary.
  6. Adjusting what a team member can access.

Proposed usability testing

The next step would be to test these workflows with family caregivers and professional caregivers. Key questions would include:

  • Can users quickly identify what needs attention?
  • Do they understand the difference between an assigned and accepted task?
  • Can they create a handoff without overlooking important details?
  • Do the care insights feel useful, understandable, and appropriately cautious?
  • Can users confidently manage access to sensitive information?

Success metrics to evaluate

  • Time required to create a handoff
  • Task assignment and completion success rates
  • Accuracy of users' understanding of task ownership
  • Number of important care details missed during handoff exercises
  • User-reported confidence in care coordination
  • Ease-of-use and trust ratings

Before a real-world launch, the product would also need robust authentication, secure data handling, verified access controls, and healthcare privacy review.

08. Outcome

FROM SCATTERED UPDATES TO A CONNECTED CAREGIVING EXPERIENCE

The outcome of this project is an interactive mobile prototype that demonstrates how multiple caregiving activities can work together within one shared experience. The design brings together:

  • A prioritized daily care dashboard
  • A chronological care activity timeline
  • Collaborative task management
  • Medication and appointment tracking
  • Structured caregiver handoff summaries
  • Care insights supported by recorded observations
  • Team messaging and configurable access preferences

The most important design outcome is the caregiver handoff workflow. By organizing completed activities, observations, pending responsibilities, and upcoming appointments into a reviewable summary, the concept offers a more structured alternative to relying entirely on memory or informal messages.

The prototype demonstrates the intended user experience; improvements in care outcomes, time savings, and caregiver confidence have not yet been measured.

09. Reflection

GOOD CARE COORDINATION IS ABOUT CREATING CLARITY AND CONFIDENCE

This project helped me explore how thoughtful UX design can simplify an emotionally demanding, information-heavy experience. One of my biggest takeaways was that caregivers do not necessarily need more information. They need information that is relevant, understandable, and actionable. Three principles became especially important:

Design for real-life interruptions

Caregivers may be balancing several responsibilities, so the interface should support quick check-ins and low-effort updates.

Make accountability visible

Clear task ownership can help teams understand what has been requested, accepted, and completed.

Keep people in control

Automated summaries and insights can help organize information, but caregivers should be able to review details and decide what to share.

What I would improve next

I would prioritize usability research with caregivers, refine the handoff workflow based on observed behavior, and test accessibility with older adults and users with varying digital confidence. I would also explore more robust notification settings, caregiver-specific views, reliable multi-user synchronization, and stronger privacy controls.

Ultimately, Care Handoff reinforced my belief that the best digital experiences do more than organize information. They help people feel more confident, connected, and supported.

Initial findings

The gap: life admin built for two. Private and shared in one calm place. That is Tandem.

Goals

For users

For the product
